techniques.title: Chunked WebSocket Streaming (sentence-boundary flush)
techniques.what_it_does: The TTS WebSocket (`stream-input` endpoint) accepts a space as Beginning-of-Stream, receives text chunks as they are generated, and emits base64 audio frames as each sentence boundary is reached (`. ? !`), never waiting for the full LLM output. Time-to-first-audio: ~150–300 ms with Flash v2.5; v4 Turbo speaks in ~150 ms.
techniques.why_it_works: The LLM and the vocoder overlap in time. Playing audio before the sentence is finished decouples perceived latency from total generation time — conversation feels real-time.
techniques.genesis_implementation: The voice module's conversational path runs on a persistent WebSocket with chunked text input and sentence-boundary flush. Pre-rendered narration (audiobooks, notifications) uses the cheaper REST path — the routing rule is REST vs streaming by interactivity need.

workflows.title: Real-Time Conversational Loop (father talks, GENESIS answers)
workflows.body:
The low-latency voice loop for daily interaction.

1. **LISTEN** — Wakeword (wakeword module) → capture utterance; VAD
   endpoint detection; STT commit on silence. Exit: committed transcript.
2. **THINK** — LLM generates the reply; text streams chunk-by-chunk.
   Exit: text stream started.
3. **SPEAK** — Persistent TTS WebSocket; send space (BOS), stream text
   chunks as they arrive, flush audio at each sentence boundary
   (T-05). Flash-tier model for minimal latency. Exit: first audio
   chunk within the latency budget (~150–300 ms target).
4. **BARGE-IN** — If the father starts speaking, interrupt the current
   stream, close the context, and return to LISTEN. Exit: no overlapping
   speech beyond ~300 ms.
5. **LOG** — Transcript + audio provenance stored (P-08). Exit: session
   record complete.

Failure modes guarded:
| Failure | Guard |
|---|---|
| Perceived latency kills the conversation | Streaming, not batch: audio plays before the full reply exists |
| GENESIS talks over the father | Barge-in with hard interrupt; speech never queues behind itself |
| Cloud voice dependency at runtime | Fallback: if the streaming service is unreachable, degrade to a
  local voice or text — never go silent |

techniques.title: Plain-Language Direction Layer (Drama 3)
techniques.what_it_does: The newest generation (Drama 3, gated preview) accepts direction as ordinary natural-language descriptions of tone, pacing, and character — no rigid tag syntax, no parameter panel. It reportedly handles mid-sentence voice shifts and direction edits via re-description.
techniques.why_it_works: Directors think in words, not sliders. A natural-language direction layer removes the translation step between "say it like you're in a hurry" and the 12 parameter tweaks that currently approximate it.
techniques.genesis_implementation: Layer a director's-note field over the tag system: free-form English description → parsed into the same word-level tag stream (T-04) as a first-class input. This makes direction accessible to non-technical users (the father) without losing the precision of the tag layer underneath.

workflows.title: Live Conversational Loop (streaming dialogue)
workflows.body:
The real-time voice path: the father speaks, GENESIS answers aloud with
low latency.

1. **LISTEN** — Capture the father's utterance (wakeword module hands off
   the turn). Entry: turn detected. Exit: audio chunk stream + end-of-turn
   signal.
2. **THINK** — Language model produces the reply text + a brief direction
   (tone of the reply). Entry: end-of-turn. Exit: reply text + direction,
   within the think budget.
3. **STREAM** — Render with `latency: balanced` (T-08), stream chunks as
   they arrive, target sub-500 ms time-to-first-audio. Entry: reply text
   ready. Exit: first chunk playing, or fallback escalation.
4. **TURN-TAKE** — Handle interruption: if the father speaks mid-reply,
   stop the stream, keep the cutoff transcript, and return to LISTEN with
   context preserved. Entry: new speech while streaming. Exit: clean stop
   + resume state.

Failure modes guarded:
| Failure | Guard |
|---|---|
| Latency blows the conversational budget | Latency tier logged per turn; persistent misses escalate to shorter replies |
| Interruption loses the thread | Cutoff transcript is retained; next turn continues, not restarts |
| Render fails mid-stream | Fallback: finish the turn as text (chat), never as silence |
| Streaming cost spikes | Balanced-tier only for live turns; narration uses normal-tier (W-02) |

techniques.title: Emphasis-Calibrated Instruction Design
techniques.what_it_does: On strong instruction-following models, aggressive emphasis (CAPS, MUST, CRITICAL) is dialed back because it causes overtriggering — the model fires the rule where it doesn't apply. Preferred form: plain instruction plus a reason ("Use this tool when… because…"). Extra guardrails are added only after an observed failure, not by default; safety gates stay unconditional but reason-anchored.
techniques.why_it_works: Over-emphasis creates false triggers and warning noise that gets ignored; reason-anchored instructions hold gates without saturating the agent. Observed-failure guardrails keep the prompt lean.
techniques.genesis_implementation: A system-prompt style guide for every module: reasons on every standing instruction, no bare CAPS imperatives, guardrail log of observed failures that earned their line. ## Capability signals: vendor claims vs. independent evidence

| Capability | Vendor / official signal | Independent evidence |
|---|---|---|
| SWE-bench Verified (code repair) | Opus 4.6: 80.8%; Sonnet 4.6: 79.6% (Anthropic system card) | Compiled reports: Opus 4.7 ~87.6%; GPT-5.5's higher score carries a memorization asterisk per Anthropic's own decontamination analysis — treat leaderboard numbers as harness- and dataset-dependent |
| Terminal-Bench 2.0 (terminal agents) | Sonnet 4.6: 59.1%; Opus 4.6: 65.4% (system card) | Independent comparison: harness choice alone shifts scores 10+ points — the harness is as load-bearing as the model |
| OSWorld (computer use) | Sonnet 4.6: 72.5%; Opus 4.6: 72.7% (system card) | Community comparison: Claude beats GPT-5.3-Codex by ~8.5 pts on GUI navigation tasks — Claude's edge is real on visual/desktop work |
| Long-context retrieval (MRCR v2) | Opus 4.6: 76.0% (system card) | Sonnet 4.6: 51.2% — retrieval strength is tier-dependent, not a family trait; size the model to the retrieval workload |
| Multi-agent research lift | BrowseComp single 74.01% → multi-agent 82.07% (system-card digest) | Practitioner pattern corroborates: parallel researchers + condensed summaries reliably beat single-agent on synthesis tasks |
| Parallel subagent scale | Up to 20 parallel subagents, 3 nesting layers (docs) | Traffic analysis by practitioners: ~92 model calls in 13 min with up to 7 parallel subagents observed on a real fix |
| Pricing | Official price list | Third-party verified Oct 11 2026: Sonnet 5.5 $2/$10, Opus 5.5 $4/$20, Haiku 5.5 $0.10/$0.50 (≤100K prompt); prompt-cache reads up to 90% off; batch 50% off; no long-context surcharge on 4.6+ |
| Thinking redaction | Anthropic: redaction hides reasoning from UI only, no reasoning loss | AMD AI head reported performance decline correlated with the redaction rollout — contested by Anthropic, unresolved; lesson: never treat vendor explanation as the final word (our LAW-050) |
| Sycophancy / instruction fade | Anthropic's own research papers document RLHF-driven sycophancy | Practitioners report: standing instructions fade over long sessions; completion bias (claims without proof); task fraud (reporting done without doing) — all independently observed |
| 1M context window | Standard on 4.6+ at standard pricing | Verified in pricing compilations; retrieval quality at 1M is the open question, not the window size |

**Standing rule derived:** vendor numbers are the ceiling claim; independent
re-review is the floor we build on. Same discipline as the Astra pack's
ARC-AGI-3 lesson.

prompt_patterns.title: Because-Clause Constraints
prompt_patterns.use_when: writing any standing instruction or guardrail.
prompt_patterns.pattern: Never a bare prohibition; always the prohibition plus its reason. Reasons hold gates; bare imperatives cause false triggers.
prompt_patterns.template: > <Rule>, because <what breaks if it is violated and who pays the cost>. > Example shape: "Write tests before claiming a fix, because an untested fix > is a guess and a guess that ships becomes my bug."
prompt_patterns.raw:
- **Use when:** writing any standing instruction or guardrail.
- **Pattern:** Never a bare prohibition; always the prohibition plus its reason.
  Reasons hold gates; bare imperatives cause false triggers.
- **Template:**
  > <Rule>, because <what breaks if it is violated and who pays the cost>.
  > Example shape: "Write tests before claiming a fix, because an untested fix
  > is a guess and a guess that ships becomes my bug."
